title: Extreme Wildfires, Distant Air Pollution, and Household Financial Health
abstract: This paper links granular wildfire burn, smoke plume, air pollution, and credit bureau data to study how extreme wildfires and distant air pollution affect household financial health. We find that households exposed to wildfire smoke—even hundreds of miles from the fire—experience significant increases in credit card delinquency and declines in credit scores. Effects are concentrated among lower-income households and in areas with higher pollution sensitivity. The results highlight wildfire smoke as an important channel through which climate risk transmits to household financial distress.

title: Credit and House Price Effects of Automated Underwriting Adoption
abstract: This paper studies how the 1990s adoption of now widely-used automated mortgage underwriting systems (AUS) affected credit access and house prices. Using variation in AUS adoption timing across lenders and markets, we find that AUS adoption expanded credit access—particularly for borrowers near approval thresholds—and increased house prices in affected markets. The results suggest that algorithmic underwriting can have significant aggregate effects on housing markets beyond the direct impact on individual loan decisions.

title: Up in Smoke: The Impact of Wildfire Pollution on Healthcare Municipal Finance
abstract: Wildfire smoke pollution is associated with significantly higher healthcare municipal borrowing costs. Using data on wildfire smoke exposure and municipal bond offerings by hospitals and health systems, we find that smoke-exposed issuers face higher yields at issuance. The effects are concentrated in areas with greater pollution exposure and among issuers with weaker balance sheets, consistent with investors pricing climate-related demand risk into healthcare municipal debt. The results highlight an underappreciated channel through which wildfire risk affects public finance.

title: The Effect of Rising Insurance Premiums on Mortgage Delinquency and Household Relocation
abstract: Using household-level microdata, this paper documents three main findings on rising homeowners insurance premiums. First, insurance premium increases cause mortgage delinquency, with effects concentrated among lower-income borrowers with limited financial buffers. Second, rising premiums induce household relocation away from high-risk areas, particularly among renters and households without strong local ties. Third, the relocation response is larger in markets with greater housing supply elasticity. The findings highlight insurance as a key mechanism through which climate risk affects household financial stability and residential sorting.

title: Audit Partners and Loan Loss Provisioning: Evidence from U.S. Bank Holding Companies
abstract: This paper uses confidential data on audit engagement partner names from bank holding company filings to study whether individual audit partners influence loan loss provisioning. Exploiting partner rotations as quasi-exogenous variation in partner assignment, we find significant partner-level effects on the timeliness and level of loan loss provisions. Partners with more conservative provisioning styles are associated with banks that recognize losses earlier and maintain higher reserves. The results suggest that individual audit partners play an important role in shaping bank financial reporting quality beyond firm-level auditor characteristics.
